title: Move the place line above the footer rule and drop the stray IMDb link
description:
The previous change put "New York City · Eastern time" on the send button's own row, reasoning that "when will she see this" is asked at the moment of deciding to send. Rendered, the argument did not survive contact with the layout: two extra text elements beside a single button read as clutter and crowded the one control the section is built around. The reasoning was right about the question and wrong about the answer's cost.

It now sits ABOVE the footer's rule, in the footer's own mono voice. Two other placements were tried and rejected first: sharing the nav's row put it between two unrelated things and made it read as an orphan, and sitting below the rule made it a second footer line competing with the signoff. Above the rule it closes the page content instead of opening the footer band, which is what a location line actually does. It carries the footer wrap's own max-width and padding so it starts on the same left edge as the nav beneath it.

The extraction is a named export, FooterPlace, rather than inline markup, so the joining rule has somewhere to live and somewhere to be tested: the parts are filtered and joined on a middot, because a middot belongs BETWEEN two parts and a single authored part must not trail one. An empty place renders nothing rather than an empty element.

SubmitRow returns to the button alone. Its `place` prop and the `.footPlace` / `.now` / `.tz` rules in Contact.module.css are gone rather than left dormant, and the isolation scenario that existed only to cover the empty-place case (`submitrow-noplace`) went with them — the component no longer has that axis to vary.

Separately, ElsewhereRow no longer hangs a small "IMDb" link off rows with a second home. It was absolutely positioned outside the row's four aligned columns, so it floated free of the grid and read as stray fine print; on mobile it was hidden outright, which is the tell that it was never load-bearing. The row now carries a single destination and the second URL stays in the content for reference. The scenario that covered it (`elsewhererow-withsecondlink`) is replaced by `elsewhererow-longtitle`, which exercises the case that actually stresses the layout — the longest title in the set, where the four columns come closest to colliding.
